item.title: China Is Getting Inflation in All the Wrong Places
item.description: China’s economy really is unique. The weak spot for the world’s second-biggest commercial power is not simply the low inflation you’ve repeatedly heard about. It’s that the type of inflation authorities are dealing with is the wrong kind.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Moss

item.title: US Chip Crackdown Could Turn Jensen Huang’s China Nightmare Into Reality
item.description: It took the spectacular ouster of Jensen Huang from Nvidia Corp. — following a romantic relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — for the Trump administration to finally crack down on some of the biggest loopholes in the artificial intelligence chips trade.For China’s AI industry, the immediate consequences will hurt. item.dc:creator: Catherine Thorbecke

item.title: Ben & Jerry’s Founders Identify the Perfect Owner: Employees
item.description: Ben & Jerry’s has long served as a model for how a brand could sell without selling out.
item.dc:creator: Beth Kowitt

item.title: James Bond Pattinson: The Bonds Who Never Got the Role
item.description: The official cinematic line of succession for James Bond since 1962 is Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, Daniel Craig and, as of this week, Robert Pattinson, the seventh canonical Agent 007. I wouldn’t be surprised if more people around the world are familiar with this lineage than the list of post-war popes. Indeed, for much of the 1970s and ‘80s, the question of who owned the role of Bond resembled the rivalry of medieval pontiffs excommunicating each
item.dc:creator: Howard Chua-Eoan

item.title: Medicaid Expansion Will Be the First Big Political Fight of 2027
item.description: November’s big Democratic wins in state races could empower the party to close the largest remaining gap in America’s healthcare safety net: Medicaid, the joint state-federal program providing healthcare for low-income Americans. Ten states have long refused to expand it, and Democrats have new power in several of them, including Texas, Georgia and Wisconsin.
item.dc:creator: Ronald Brownstein

item.title: The 60/40 Portfolio Is Still the Heavyweight Champion
item.description: If you’re worried that an unraveling of the artificial-intelligence boom — whether because of overinvestment, circular deals, energy constraints, regulation or l’affaire Jensen Huang — will sideswipe your portfolio, I have a simple solution: the timeless, dependable 60/40 portfolio.
item.dc:creator: Nir Kaissar

item.title: The Fed's 'Immaculate Disinflation' Strategy Will Fail
item.description: The Federal Reserve continues to slow walk its efforts to push down inflation. On one hand, Chair Kevin Warsh’s rhetoric about his determination to achieve the central bank’s goal of 2% inflation is strong. In the opening remarks of his press conference following the Oct. 28 Federal Open Market Committee meeting he noted:
item.dc:creator: Bill Dudley

item.title: Anthropic’s Compute Strategy Exposes Its Biggest IPO Vulnerability
item.description: With just hours to go before Anthropic PBC is due to raise some $65 billion in what will be the largest initial public offering in history, I can’t shake the feeling that it all feels like one giant roll of the dice on the AI bubble and praying a seven turns up.
item.dc:creator: Dave Lee

item.title: Trump Is Walking Into Putin and Xi's Summit Trap
item.description: If and when the world’s three most powerful men meet in Shenzhen this week, the optics will evoke ominous analogies to the Yalta Conference of 1945, when another triumvirate carved up the planet into spheres of influence.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Kluth

item.title: Anthropic Profit Is Hurt by $45 Billion of Rewards to Staff
item.description: There are lots of big numbers in Anthropic PBC’s initial public offering, but one that merits attention is the likely value of share rewards paid to its staff. The artificial intelligence firm’s profit margins look very different depending on whether this hefty chunk of the payroll is counted or ignored. Anthropic’s suffix — short for “public benefit corporation” — could just as well be “SBC,” or stock-based compensation.
item.dc:creator: Chris Hughes

item.title: Food Prices Are Up But Forecasts for a Global Food Crisis Are Wrong
item.description: Ever since the US attacked Iran, the world has been needlessly worrying about a looming food crisis. For many it has been a question of when, rather than if. In the blogosphere and in far-left corners of academia, the talk was about something far more calamitous: famine. All very scary — and all completely wrong.
item.dc:creator: Javier Blas

item.title: Ukraine War: Trump Is 0 for 10 With Gifts to Russia's Putin
item.description: Just as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow last week to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin about Ukraine, the US delivered a gift as valuable as anything they were about to say. The SpaceX Starshield modules that enable Ukrainian interceptors to bring down Russia’s jet-powered drones suddenly had their speeds limited, severely weakening Ukrainian defenses.
item.dc:creator: Marc Champion

item.title: Britain Can’t Keep Ignoring Its Quiet Quitters
item.description: Britain is undergoing an epidemic of “quiet quitting,” where employees do only the minimum required in their jobs. It’s a modern recurrence of an old problem. item.dc:creator: Matthew Brooker

item.title: Reversing Brexit: UK and EU Should Aim Higher in New Talks
item.description: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has done something British politicians have avoided for a decade: reopened the question of Brexit without pretending the answer is obvious. After Friday’s UK-EU summit, he has promised “a serious dialogue about the different options” for Britain’s long-term relationship with Europe. It’s overdue.
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: Huang Debacle Is Delivering a Stress Test
item.description: How Trump 2.0’s market aims are shaping up now.
item.dc:creator: John Authers

item.title: Service Outages Impact Banks, FAA, Microsoft — What’s Next?
item.description: First Microsoft was down, then it was the planes, now it’s the banks. What is going on?
item.dc:creator: Jessica Karl

item.title: India Inc.’s Sudden Craving for Dollars Is a Dangerous Gamble
item.description: In 1997, India narrowly escaped the Asian currency crisis that engulfed Southeast Asia because, as the International Monetary Fund noted, it had avoided the excessive dollar borrowing, especially short-term debt, that other countries had become addicted to. That prudence has remained official policy for more than three decades.
item.dc:creator: Srinivasan Sivabalan

item.title: Bond Has Robert Pattinson. Finding the Right Villain Will Be Harder
item.description: Six actors have officially worn the 007 mantle, in 25 movies spread across 60 years that yielded two truly great James Bonds: Sean Connery and Daniel Craig. As Robert Pattinson slides into the tuxedo, the next pressing question isn’t the name above the title, but rather who he’ll fight as Ian Fleming’s Cold War creation ventures further into the 21st century.
item.dc:creator: Brian Lowry

item.title: AI's Climate Change Will Destroy the Global Village to Save It
item.description: Not long ago, there was this idea that artificial intelligence could help the planet avoid the worst of global heating by using its superior brainpower to discover climate solutions humans couldn’t. Lately, though, it seems that if AI is still going to save the global village, it will first have to destroy it. With climate change.
item.dc:creator: Mark Gongloff

item.title: Measles Is Officially Back. RFK Jr. Is Making It Harder to Beat Again
item.description: Measles is endemic again in the US.
